title: Consumer Reviews and Regulation: Evidence from New York City Restaurants
eligible_reason: No qualifying design, and the package ships only synthetic data. The demand event study (Figure 6, common.R) stacks restaurant-level grade-posting events in a window of plus or minus 15 days, with event-id FE (review_id) and day-of-week FE. It compares bad events (A to B/C/pending) with other events and adds time-varying controls (yelp_stars, a_card, has_rating, has_card). That is a stacked event-window design with controls and no calendar-time FE. Tables 3-4 are violation-level regressions of violation indicators on review availability x informativeness, with inspection FE and IV versions. Table 1 is a cross-sectional inspection-score regression.
design_notes: src/common.R: reg_es = feols(sold_out_30 ~ yelp_stars + a_card + has_rating + has_card + t_factor*bad_sr | review_id + dow, cluster=camis), and reg_did with post*bad_sr. src/tab_4_A6_A7_A8.R: feols(violation_yn ~ has_rev_t*informative | inspectionid + violcode/violcamis_fe), with 2SLS versions instrumented by cumulative reviewer activity. src/tab_A9_A10.R: OLS/logit/probit of inspector-reviewer independence. The remaining code is DMR text models and LightGBM prediction.
software_notes: R (fixest) for tables and event study; Python for DMR and prediction models.
screener_notes: Screened from package only. The README states that all inputs are synthetic data that preserve statistical properties, and that results will differ numerically from the paper.
